title: Three Underused X-Men Villains Who Could Carry Solo Movies
excerpt:
Emma Frost, Juggernaut and Sabretooth headline a new argument for deeper MCU stories.
These are editorial proposals, not announced Marvel Studios productions.
body_md:
As the X-Men move toward a new era within the Marvel Cinematic Universe, attention naturally turns to which heroes will be introduced. Yet the mutant franchise also has an unusually rich roster of antagonists, many of whom received limited development during the years when 20th Century Fox controlled the film rights. A new editorial argues that three characters deserve more than another brief supporting appearance.

Emma Frost is the first choice. In the comics, the White Queen has a complicated history that includes elite social circles, the Hellfire Club, conflicts with the X-Men and eventual alliances with them. January Jones portrayed her in X-Men: First Class, but the writer argues that the film reduced a potentially fascinating character to a relatively thin role.

A solo story could explore Emma's wealthy and troubled family background, her rise within the Hellfire Club and the personal choices that shaped her identity. Introducing her first as an antagonist could also create a more meaningful foundation for any later relationship with the X-Men. That is a proposed creative direction, not a reported studio plan.

Juggernaut is the second candidate. Cain Marko is Charles Xavier's stepbrother in the comics and gains tremendous power through the Crimson Gem of Cyttorak. His appearance in X-Men: The Last Stand offered little explanation of that origin or his relationship with Xavier. A standalone movie could investigate how he found the gem, how he responded to his transformation and what his new power cost him.

The third selection is Sabretooth, also known as Victor Creed. His brutal rivalry with Wolverine is central to many comic stories, but the films have used him unevenly. Tyler Mane portrayed the character in the original X-Men, while Liev Schreiber took the role in X-Men Origins: Wolverine. The writer particularly praises Schreiber's interpretation and regrets that it was not developed further in later movies.

A character-focused Sabretooth film could explore his violent past, his psychological relationship with Wolverine and his own worldview rather than treating him simply as a physical obstacle. The same broader principle applies to all three choices: an effective antagonist can be compelling because of personal motivations and contradictions, not just powers.

None of these films is announced or confirmed in the source. The article is an opinion piece identifying opportunities for the MCU to reinterpret characters whose previous screen versions the writer considers disappointing. Whether Marvel eventually pursues any of them remains an open question.
